figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Examples of textile fragments from the Oseberg ship burial (834 CE). These degraded fragments present significant challenges for computational reconstruction. The fragments do not correspond to their true scale. Images by George Alexis Pantos, Museum of Cultural History, University of Oslo.Photographs of six archaeological textile fragments from the Oseberg ship burial, arranged on a black background. Each fragment is irregular in outline, torn at the edges and heavily faded, with woven figures, animals and geometric borders still partly visible in brown, gray and reddish tones.
figures.headline: Six photographs of Oseberg fragments show fading, tears and irregular outlines that make reassembly hard.
citing_sentences: The fragments are now housed at the Museum of Cultural History in Oslo, where ongoing efforts seek to understand their original configurations (Figure 1).
The 45 Oseberg fragment images carry genuine archaeological damage: the fading, staining, holes, and irregular outlines visible in Figure 1.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: UMAP projection of CLIP embeddings for the textile collection, colored by MET curatorial department, as displayed in the FiftyOne curation interface. Natural clusters emerge, enabling systematic identification of outliers and quality issues.Scatter plot of a two-dimensional UMAP projection of CLIP image embeddings on a dark background, where each point is one textile image colored by MET curatorial department. The points form one large dense cluster and one smaller separate cluster with scattered outliers around them. A legend lists fifteen departments, including Asian Art, Costume Institute, Islamic Art, Medieval Art and The Cloisters.
figures.headline: A UMAP projection of CLIP embeddings separates the textile images into one dense cluster, one smaller cluster and scattered outliers.
citing_sentences: Figure 2 shows the UMAP projection of CLIP embeddings, revealing natural clusters that guided systematic quality assessment.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Overview of the final curated TEXMET dataset showing 18,644 high-quality textile images spanning diverse historical periods and cultural traditions.A dense grid of thumbnail images from the curated TEXMET dataset, each labeled with its object title. The thumbnails show tapestries, woven panels, rank badges, embroidered hangings and textile fragments from many periods and cultures, in both color and black and white.
figures.headline: A grid of thumbnails from the final dataset shows tapestries, woven panels and fragments from many periods and cultures.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 provides an overview of the final curated dataset.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: JPDVT architecture showing the Vision Transformer backbone integrated with the diffusion process for position prediction. Figure by the authors, created using Canva.Two-part pipeline diagram of JPDVT. On the left, the training path: image patches are shuffled, their position embeddings are noised by forward diffusion, and the patches pass through a linear projection of flattened patches and reverse diffusion transformer layers that output the predicted patch ordering. On the right, the testing path: visible patches, missing patches and Gaussian noise pass through the same transformer layers for T iterations, generating the missing patches and reassembling the complete textile image.
figures.headline: The JPDVT pipeline noises position embeddings, denoises them through transformer layers, and outputs a predicted patch ordering.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: FCViT architecture illustrating the coordinate regression process where fragment positions are directly predicted. Figure by the authors, created using Canva.Flow diagram of FCViT. An input image is divided into a 3 by 3 grid of fragments with ground-truth coordinates, the fragments are shuffled, and the shuffled patches pass through an encoder and a coordinate predictor that outputs a predicted row and column coordinate for each fragment. The predicted coordinates are used to reassemble the image, and a loss term compares predicted coordinates with true coordinates.
figures.headline: The FCViT pipeline predicts a row and column coordinate for each shuffled patch and compares them with true coordinates in its loss.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: DiffAssemble architecture demonstrating the graph-based diffusion approach for 2D puzzle reassembly. Figure by the authors, created using Canva.Diagram of DiffAssemble. Puzzle pieces are embedded by a rotation-equivariant 2D encoder, each piece becomes a graph node combining its feature vector with position and rotation values at diffusion step t, and an attention-based graph neural network denoises the node attributes to step t minus 1. Below, four snapshots show the pieces moving from scattered at t equals T to a fully assembled image at t equals 0, with arrows marking forward diffusion during training and reverse denoising at inference.
figures.headline: The DiffAssemble pipeline denoises piece poses in a graph network, moving scattered pieces into an assembled image over diffusion steps.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: DiffAssemble reconstruction examples on CelebA-HQ (Karras et al., 2018) across puzzle sizes (6$\times$6 to 12$\times$12). Left: successful reconstructions showing correct piece placement. Right: failure cases revealing common error patterns.Two side-by-side galleries of DiffAssemble reconstructions of CelebA-HQ face images at puzzle sizes 6 by 6, 8 by 8, 10 by 10 and 12 by 12. Each column shows the scrambled pieces, the model's reconstruction and the ground-truth image. On the left, success cases place every piece correctly: 36 of 36, 64 of 64, 100 of 100 and 144 of 144. On the right, failure cases degrade as the puzzle grows: 35 of 36 (97.2 percent), 62 of 64 (96.9 percent), 87 of 100 (87.0 percent) and 111 of 144 (77.1 percent).
figures.headline: On CelebA-HQ, DiffAssemble places every piece correctly in its success cases, while failures worsen as puzzles grow from 6 by 6 to 12 by 12.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 presents qualitative examples of DiffAssemble reconstructions across multiple puzzle sizes, illustrating both successful assemblies and failure cases.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Baseline performance comparison of JPDVT, FCViT, and DiffAssemble on ImageNet 3$\times$3 puzzles showing puzzle and fragment accuracy.Grouped bar chart of baseline accuracy on ImageNet 3 by 3 puzzles for three models, with paired bars for puzzle accuracy and fragment accuracy. JPDVT reaches 67.89 percent puzzle accuracy and 80.02 percent fragment accuracy, FCViT 68.78 and 84.21 percent, and DiffAssemble 56.61 and 84.03 percent.
figures.headline: On ImageNet 3 by 3 puzzles, DiffAssemble has the lowest puzzle accuracy at 56.61 percent, though its fragment accuracy stays at 84.03 percent.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Cross-dataset evaluation comparing model performance on ImageNet, TEXMET, and Oseberg fragments. DiffAssemble maintains performance while FCViT collapses, demonstrating the domain gap between natural images and historical textiles.Grouped bar chart of puzzle accuracy for three models on three datasets. JPDVT scores 67.89 percent on ImageNet, 32.92 percent on TEXMET and 20.00 percent on Oseberg fragments. FCViT scores 68.78, 8.30 and 24.44 percent. DiffAssemble scores 56.61, 65.08 and 26.67 percent. FCViT's TEXMET bar is by far the shortest, while DiffAssemble is the only model whose textile accuracy exceeds its ImageNet accuracy.
figures.headline: FCViT falls to 8.30 percent on TEXMET, while DiffAssemble is the only model that scores higher on TEXMET than on ImageNet.
citing_sentences: Figure 9 visualizes this domain gap, illustrating DiffAssemble’s superior robustness to distribution shift compared to transformer-based approaches.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Summary of DiffAssemble puzzle accuracy across the five experimental stages. Fine-tuning on TEXMET lifts accuracy in both evaluation domains: TEXMET rises from 65.08% to 85.89% and the held-out Oseberg fragments from 26.67% to 64.44%, indicating that the learned representations transfer to degraded archaeological materials. The drop between the third and fourth stages reflects the switch to the much harder Oseberg domain, not a decline in the model.Line chart of DiffAssemble puzzle accuracy across five experimental stages: ImageNet baseline 56.61 percent, TEXMET generalization 65.08 percent, TEXMET fine-tuned 85.89 percent, Oseberg generalization 26.67 percent and Oseberg fine-tuned 64.44 percent. The line climbs to a peak at the third stage, drops sharply at the fourth stage where the evaluation domain changes to Oseberg, then rises again. Two callout boxes note a gain of 20.8 points from fine-tuning on TEXMET and a gain of 37.8 points on Oseberg.
figures.headline: Fine-tuning DiffAssemble on TEXMET raises its Oseberg puzzle accuracy from 26.67 percent to 64.44 percent across five experimental stages.
citing_sentences: Figure 10 summarizes performance across the five experimental stages, showing that fine-tuning improves accuracy on both TEXMET and the held-out Oseberg evaluation set.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: The masking and inpainting pipeline on ImageNet validation images. Top: regular centered-rectangle mask. Bottom: irregular mask derived from a single Oseberg fragment. Panels left to right: original image, mask, masked image, and ASUKA-inpainted result. The inpainted images restore visual plausibility to the masked regions.Two rows of four panels showing the masking and inpainting pipeline on ImageNet validation images. The top row uses a photograph of a construction crane with a regular centered rectangular mask covering 35.63 percent of the image. The bottom row uses a photograph of a graffiti-covered freight wagon with an irregular blob-shaped mask derived from an Oseberg fragment, covering 35.69 percent. In each row the panels are, from left to right, the original image, the binary mask, the masked image with the removed region shown in black, and the ASUKA-inpainted result, which restores a visually plausible scene.
figures.headline: Regular and Oseberg-derived irregular masks cover 35.63 percent and 35.69 percent of example images before inpainting.
citing_sentences: Figure 11 illustrates the full pipeline for both mask types, from the original image to the inpainted result; quantitative fidelity metrics, which show that irregular masks are consistently harder to inpaint, are reported in the supplementary material.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Inpainting effectiveness: comparison of puzzle accuracy before (masked) and after inpainting for each model under both masking conditions.Two grouped bar charts comparing puzzle accuracy on masked images against inpainted images for each model, using 1,000 images per condition at 3 by 3. Under the regular mask, JPDVT moves from 87.3 to 86.1 percent (down 1.2 points), FCViT from 60.8 to 65.1 percent (up 4.3) and DiffAssemble from 50.5 to 58.5 percent (up 8.0). Under the irregular mask, JPDVT moves from 79.1 to 84.3 percent (up 5.2), FCViT from 46.1 to 60.1 percent (up 14.0) and DiffAssemble from 54.7 to 57.9 percent (up 3.2).
figures.headline: Inpainting raises FCViT puzzle accuracy under irregular masks from 46.1 percent to 60.1 percent, but lowers JPDVT under regular masks.
citing_sentences: Figure 12 shows that inpainting is a useful but not universal recovery strategy, and its benefit depends on both the model and the mask type.

figures.caption: The ten Oseberg fragment images best reordered by an ImageNet-trained baseline model. Each fragment photograph is divided into a 3$\times$3 grid and reassembled in isolation; nine of the ten are restored completely (9/9 patches) and one partially (7/9). Fragments with distinctive global structure survive severe degradation even under the baseline model, within this simplified setting.Grid of ten photographs of Oseberg textile fragments on black backgrounds, each overlaid with a 3 by 3 grid marking how it was split and reassembled. figures.headline: Nine of the ten best-reordered Oseberg fragments are fully restored by the ImageNet-trained baseline in the 3 by 3 setting.
citing_sentences: We evaluated all models on the 45 Oseberg textile fragments to establish baseline performance on real archaeological materials (see Figure 13 for examples of 3$\times$3 fragmented Oseberg puzzles).

Figure 13 presents the Oseberg fragment images most successfully reordered by the baseline model, illustrating that fragments with distinctive global structure remain solvable despite severe degradation.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: FCViT 3$\times$3 puzzle-solving results on ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009). Top: successful reconstruction (9/9 pieces correct). citing_sentences: The regression formulation lacks explicit uniqueness constraints, making it prone to duplicate placements where multiple fragments are assigned similar coordinates (Figure 14).

abstract: The reconstruction of fragmented historical textiles presents a significant challenge in computational archaeology. The Oseberg ship burial, dating to 834 CE, yielded hundreds of degraded textile fragments that have resisted systematic computational analysis. While deep learning has revolutionized image-based puzzle solving, progress on archaeological textiles has been limited by the lack of domain-specific datasets and systematic evaluation of modern architectures. To address this gap, we present TEXMET, a curated dataset of 18,644 historical textile images from the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Open Access collection, representing the first textile-specific benchmark for puzzle-solving research. Using TEXMET, we conduct a systematic evaluation of three state-of-the-art puzzle-solving models: JPDVT, FCViT, and DiffAssemble. Our experiments reveal that the transformer-based models pre-trained on standard datasets fail to generalize to textiles, but domain-specific fine-tuning proves highly effective. The graph-based DiffAssemble model, when fine-tuned on TEXMET, achieves 85.89% puzzle accuracy on textile data. Most significantly, applying this fine-tuned model to 45 highly degraded Oseberg fragments yields a performance increase from 26.67% to 64.44% puzzle accuracy. These results establish TEXMET as a new benchmark for textile reconstruction and demonstrate that domain adaptation is essential for applying puzzle-solving methods to imagery of real archaeological materials.

sections.body: Oseberg textile fragments from the 9th-century ship burial are hundreds in number and degraded, and no large textile-specific dataset existed for puzzle-solving research. The authors introduce TEXMET, a set of 18,644 Metropolitan Museum of Art textile images, and run the first systematic evaluation of JPDVT, FCViT and DiffAssemble on textiles. Transformer models pre-trained on standard datasets fail to generalize to textiles. Fine-tuning DiffAssemble on TEXMET reaches 85.89% puzzle accuracy on TEXMET and raises accuracy on Oseberg fragments from 26.67% to 64.44%. The authors describe the work as a benchmarking and domain adaptation study, a controlled first step rather than a complete reconstruction solution.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Oseberg textile fragments lack a textile puzzle benchmark, so the authors build TEXMET and test three puzzle models.

sections.body: Classical puzzle methods used shape and color cues and worked best on undamaged, uniform pieces. Deep learning revived puzzle solving as a self-supervised task, and transformers followed. Heritage studies include Paumard and colleagues on artwork edge matching, Derech and colleagues on eroded artifacts, and Funkhouser and colleagues on fresco fragments. Earlier Oseberg work used deep features and texture descriptors, an interactive software tool, and retrieval under irregular masking. Existing datasets consist of natural images, fresco fragments, or intact modern fabrics. The authors state that no large public historical textile dataset existed and that no systematic evaluation of modern architectures on textiles had been published.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier puzzle work targeted clean pieces, and no prior study evaluated modern deep models on historical textiles.

sections.body: TEXMET was built from the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Open Access collection under a CC0 license, using the MET REST API. The harvest queried 33,588 objects, 27,373 of which had images, and yielded 55,007 total images. CLIP ViT-B/32 embeddings and UMAP projections in FiftyOne guided quality review. Samples were classified as poor quality or noise, and 8,716 were removed, of which 2,567 were duplicate images. The final set of 18,644 images is 68.1% of the original collection, averages 1,557 × 1,631 pixels at 3.3 MP, and is 92.0% color (RGB). The split is 14,915, 1,864 and 1,865. European Sculpture and Decorative Arts contributes 45.7%. The comparison table lists its fragmentation as simulated.
sections.heading: The TEXMET Dataset
sections.headline: TEXMET holds 18,644 Metropolitan Museum textile images after the authors removed 8,716 poor or noisy samples.

sections.body: The section defines puzzle solving as predicting each fragment's grid position. JPDVT treats positions as a conditional diffusion problem: a Vision Transformer encodes fragments and a diffusion process predicts positional encodings, with mask tokens for missing pieces. FCViT drops permutations and regresses horizontal and vertical coordinates for each fragment with a smooth L1 loss. The text lists duplicate placements as a limitation, because the loss has no uniqueness constraint. DiffAssemble represents pieces as graph nodes, uses a graph neural network inside a diffusion denoiser, and predicts translations and rotations, with one 26.7M parameter model covering 6×6 to 12×12 puzzles. Puzzle accuracy requires every piece to be correct, while piece accuracy counts individual pieces.
sections.heading: Methods
sections.headline: Three puzzle models are described: JPDVT as diffusion, FCViT as coordinate regression, and DiffAssemble as graph diffusion.

sections.body: Three datasets are used: ImageNet-1k with 1,281,167 natural images, TEXMET with 14,915, 1,864 and 1,865 images for training, validation and test, and 45 Oseberg fragments with an average masked area of 75.60%. Models follow their original training protocols. DiffAssemble was trained on CelebA-HQ for 158 epochs, and fine-tuning ran for 150 more epochs on TEXMET. Each puzzle is one image cut into a G by G grid with a seeded permutation, with no rotations and no missing pieces. TEXMET splits are object-level, but the authors note that related fabrics from one source may cross splits. Oseberg fragments are cut into 3×3 grids and solved in isolation. Inscribed crops, with 206 manually annotated squares, test whether models use shape cues. Results come from a single run per configuration.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Models are tested on ImageNet, TEXMET and 45 Oseberg fragments, with seeded splits and single runs per configuration.

sections.body: ImageNet-trained DiffAssemble reaches 65.08% puzzle accuracy on TEXMET without fine-tuning, while JPDVT drops to 32.92% and FCViT to 8.30%. On the 45 Oseberg fragments, baseline puzzle accuracy is 20.00% for JPDVT, 24.44% for FCViT and 26.67% for DiffAssemble. Fine-tuning DiffAssemble raises TEXMET accuracy to 85.89% and Oseberg accuracy to 64.44%. After fine-tuning, JPDVT falls to 10.88% on TEXMET, and FCViT rises only to 10.86%. For the fine-tuned model, inscribed crops that remove shape cues lower Oseberg accuracy to 39.81%, which the authors read as learned textile patterns. Inpainting helps some model and mask combinations and not others. JPDVT falls from 32.92% to 9.54% on TEXMET at 4×4. The FCViT reproduction on ImageNet was 10 percentage points below its published result.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Fine-tuning DiffAssemble lifts Oseberg puzzle accuracy from 26.67% to 64.44%, while JPDVT and FCViT do not adapt.

sections.body: The authors attribute DiffAssemble's advantage to its graph representation, which captures local connectivity, and to iterative diffusion refinement, which they say helps with degraded material. They attribute FCViT's collapse to its regression formulation and lack of uniqueness constraints. Fragment realism is assessed qualitatively. TEXMET tiles have zero masked area and regular square geometry, while real Oseberg fragments average 75.60% masked area and a mean compactness of 0.15. A distractor experiment with 16 candidates failed at the implementation stage for all three models. The authors cite Berels, who also found retrieval degrades under irregular masking. Stated limitations include grid puzzles only, isolated Oseberg fragments without cross-fragment ground truth, only 45 fragments, and simulated cuts that may not match real fragmentation.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The authors attribute DiffAssemble's advantage to its graph structure and argue that missing training data, not architecture, limited transfer.

sections.body: The paper lists four contributions: the TEXMET dataset of 18,644 images, the first systematic evaluation of three architectures on textiles and Oseberg fragments, evidence that domain fine-tuning is essential, and a planned release of code, checkpoints and data. Key findings include a large domain gap for transformer models, the DiffAssemble advantage, and a 37.77 percentage point gain on Oseberg fragments after fine-tuning. Inscribed-crop results are read as evidence of learned textile features. Future work names irregular fragment handling, full tapestry reconstruction, other heritage materials and larger datasets. The text states that code, checkpoints and data will be made public, not that they already are.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The authors conclude that domain fine-tuning is essential, while irregular shapes and cross-fragment matching remain open.
